newsitem.title: CANADA: Manley to call for Canadian satellite TV bids.
newsitem.headline: Manley to call for Canadian satellite TV bids.

text.p: Canadian Industry Minister John Manley on Tuesday said that in about a week he would invite Canadian companies to bid for the ownership and operation of two satellites from a Canadian orbital slot.

Manley's statement came hours after the U.S. Federal Communications Commission denied a bid by Telquest Ventures and Tele-Communications Inc to beam TV programs across the United States through two Canadian satellites which were to be owned and operated by Telesat Canada.

"My belief is that the time has come for us to proceed with a possible Canada-only solution and my hope is that there will be some companies that will be able to pursue that, including Telesat," Manley told reporters after a parliamentary session.

He said that late Monday he sent a letter to Montreal-based Telesat, telling the company that if the FCC rejected the Telquest/TCI bid, he would revoke the permission Industry Canada gave to Telesat to have access to the two satellite slots.
"We will launch a process probably in a week or so to invite applications for the use of the slots," Manley said.
Telesat is owned by Alouette Telecommunications Ltd, which is 57 percent-held by BCE Inc. The rest is held by Canadian telephone companies and by Spar Aerospace Ltd.
Manley said he was disappointed with the FCC decision, but was confident that there were Canadian companies capable of putting forward solid bids for the satellite slots.
Asked who those companies might be, Manley said Telesat remained a strong contender and mentioned Shaw Communications Inc as a likely bidder.
The FCC said its decision was based on its policy to dismiss applications for Direct Broadcast Satellites (DBS) when a company's satellites had not yet been licensed.

But Manley said Canada's approval of the satellite licenses was conditional on a favorable FCC decision. The FCC said Telquest and TCI could refile their applications once the satellites were licensed by the Canadian government.
In a news release, Telesat reaffirmed its decision to pursue the bid to provide direct-to-home satellite television.
"One way or another, Telesat will eventually be a provider of direct-to-home satellite facilities right across North America," Telesat president and chief executive Larry Boisvert said.
-- Malina Poshtova Zang, Reuters Ottawa Bureau (613) 235-6745
